blocks.text: The aspiring model Vera von Lehndorff created “Veruschka” – little Vera – as a memorable alternative persona whose existence was performance art.

She used her natural resources: a 6ft-plus-tall body that, horizontal, could fill an entire glossy magazine spread; a face with magnificent bone architecture and feline eyes; and a long mane that was amenable to brutal short cuts and extraordinary coiffures. All were animated by her instinct for making shapes in air – not a model’s poses but a dancer’s movements that only a click of the lens could catch. Watch her seducing the camera of the photographer, played by David Hemmings , in Michelangelo Antonioni ’s 1966 film Blow Up to see her original act in action.

blocks.alt: Veruschka with David Hemmings in Michelangelo Antonioni’s Blow Up, 1966.
blocks.caption: Veruschka with David Hemmings in Michelangelo Antonioni’s Blow Up, 1966. Photograph: Photo 12/Alamy

blocks.text: These gifts made Veruschka, who has died aged 87, one of fashion’s greatest stars for 15 years, with hundreds of magazine covers (she did not keep count), many for Vogue. She was just what the new empress editor of American Vogue, Diana Vreeland , wanted in order to express the exotic aspects of 1960s culture. When first introduced to the young model, Vreeland pinned her photo to her wall and declared: “You’re going to hear from me.”

Veruschka was a big, and deep, enough “character” to sustain Vreeland’s wild fantasies, including a legendary 1966 sequence shot by Richard Avedon in Hokkaido, Japan’s “snow country”, a cinematic epic with Veruschka wrapped in a zoo’s-worth of furs plus an 8ft-long Dynel wig. Vreeland wanted it to be 20 feet. Veruschka could have carried that off too.

Nothing seemed preposterous with Veruschka in focus: for fun she attended Woodstock in 1969, in multiple necklaces and a minimal bra, and every camera gravitated to her. Vreeland went so far as to allow Veruschka and her then lover, the photographer Franco Rubartelli, to come up with their own mad ideas, such as a moonlit shoot on Christmas Day on the island of Eleuthera in the Bahamas; he also snapped her adventuring in an Yves Saint Laurent safari jacket in 1968, an image that established the designer’s bold-woman credentials.

blocks.text: Besides Avedon, who thought her the most beautiful woman in the world, other Vogue photographers, from the old-school Horst P Horst and Irving Penn to Bert Stern and David Bailey, enjoyed collaboration with Veruschka, open to any experiment except smiling, though Steven Meisel did at last capture her surprisingly goofy grin.

It had been an Italian photographer, Johnny Moncada, who helped Vera create Veruschka. The photographer Ugo Mulas had spotted her beauty when she was studying art in Florence in 1959, but Paris turned her away for being too tall, and the New York agency chief Eileen Ford advised her to starve on hard-boiled eggs, then rejected her.

Back in Italy, she and Moncada did sporadic jobs together over a year, and when those pictures were published in 2014 as a book, From Vera to Veruschka , she remembered how he developed her on-camera persona by encouraging her to reveal her real feelings: “Having a look of sadness in my eyes is my biggest problem … he allowed me to be myself, even if that meant looking melancholy.”

Her life had had much to be sad about. She was born the daughter of Count Heinrich von Lehndorff-Steinort, with a family castle on their estate in Steinort, East Prussia: he was executed in 1944 for his part in the July plot to assassinate Hitler. The Gestapo imprisoned his pregnant wife, Gottliebe von Kalnein, and sent young Vera and her sisters, Gabriele and Marie, to an SS-run children’s home in Bad Sachsa. They were reunited with their mother and new sister, Catharina, after the war’s end, but were homeless and shunned in Germany. They lived wherever a relative took them in, which meant 13 different schools in which the spidery, long and thin Vera was always an outsider.

None of this was known to the fashion world, which easily accepted the vaguely eastern European identity suggested by the pseudonym Veruschka, and took advantage of her metier for metamorphosis. The 60s were the era of the international “Beautiful People”, and Veruschka was the fairest of them all.

Yet even during her peak years, when she commanded an unprecedented $10,000 a day, she wanted to dissolve into the background, and on shoots camouflaged herself with shoe polish to disappear into a Kenyan landscape, or used body paint to match herself to a floor.

blocks.alt: Veruschka in a shoot for Vogue, 1966.
blocks.caption: Veruschka in a shoot for Vogue, 1966. She finally gave up on fashion in 1975. Photograph: Bert Stern/Condé Nast/Getty Images

blocks.text: She finally gave up on fashion in 1975, after Grace Mirabella , who had deposed Vreeland as Vogue editor and was under orders to democratise the magazine, told her that she needed to be more ordinary, what we would call “relatable”. Veruschka interpreted that as more bourgeois and stalked away in her usual flat shoes.

Thereafter, she lived under her own name as the simultaneous artist’s model and artist she had intended to be, using her body for a canvas. She had worked with the photographer Holger Trülzsch from 1970. He painted her to blend into surrounding natural surfaces for fine art photographs, and then in 1978 for performances where she absorbed herself into old buildings. They also played with painting clothes directly on to her body, an exploration of, and revenge for, her years of exposure to fashion. Trülzsch and Veruschka published a monograph of their work, Trans-figurations, in 1986, with a foreword by Susan Sontag .
As an artist she led a simple life in Brooklyn and, from 2005, in suburban Berlin, where she wrote an autobiography, Veruschka: Mein Leben, published in 2011.

Fashion asked her back occasionally, paying well for her to parade on a show catwalk, something she had not done in her glory years. She did not care whether the designers were unknowns or Karl Lagerfeld at Chanel, as she had never liked couture. Her personal style remained haute hippy, almost any length of cloth or exaggerated makeup looking elegant on her frame and face. In a late appearance, aged nearly 80, in denim and worn leather for Acne Studios, she was as cool and beyond it all as ever.
Her sisters Gabriele and Catharina survive her.
